Introduction to mixeff

Source: vignettes/mixeff.Rmd
mixeff.Rmd
library(mixeff)

mixeff fits linear and generalized linear mixed models in R using the mixeff-rs Rust engine. If you use lme4, the formula syntax and functions such as fixef(), ranef(), VarCorr(), predict(), and summary() will be familiar. Supported models are listed by supported_models(); differences in arguments and output are described in vignette("lme4-migration").

The fitted object stores the model specification, convergence diagnostics, and the method used for each inference result. You can inspect a singular fit, find out which tests are available, and save the results for later use. This vignette demonstrates those steps on a small repeated-measures dataset, then explains model support and the requirements for restoring a saved fit.

Tests compare mixeff with lme4 on the datasets shipped with the package, using documented numerical tolerances. The benchmarking article reports timing comparisons and simulation results, with the package versions and model designs used in each study.

The dataset

We simulate 10 daily reaction-time measurements for each of 18 subjects. The subject intercepts and slopes are nearly perfectly correlated by construction. This example produces a singular fit in both lme4 and mixeff.

set.seed(3)
n_subj <- 18L
days   <- 0:9
b0     <- rnorm(n_subj, sd = 30)
b1     <- 0.5 * b0 / 30 * 10 + rnorm(n_subj, sd = 0.5)

sleep_like <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_subj), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    subj = factor(i),
    days = days,
    rt   = 250 + b0[i] + (10 + b1[i]) * days +
           rnorm(length(days), sd = 20)
  )
}))

head(sleep_like, 4)
#>   subj days       rt
#> 1    1    0 247.1492
#> 2    1    1 227.7095
#> 3    1    2 213.1613
#> 4    1    3 254.4247

Fitting a model

The formula below estimates a population slope for days and allows each subject to have a different intercept and slope.

fit <- lmm(
  rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj),
  sleep_like,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)
fit
#> Linear mixed model fit by REML
#> Formula: rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj)
#> Fit status: converged_reduced_rank
#> Optimizer: trust_bq; iterations: 30; objective: 1647.7
#> nobs: 180, sigma: 20.065, logLik: -823.849
#> Fixed effects:
#> (Intercept)        days 
#>   239.87900     9.25095 
#> 
#> Fitted covariance state:
#> The fitted covariance matrix is rank-deficient.
#>   r0: requested rank 2; fitted effective rank 1.
#> Use changes(fit) to see which dimension was unsupported.
#> Use random_options(spec, group = subj) to inspect lower-dimensional covariance choices.
#> Audit verbs: audit(), diagnostics(), inference_table(), model_report()

fixef(), ranef(), VarCorr(), predict(), simulate(), anova(), and summary() all work on this fit; vignette("lme4-migration") lists where their output differs from lme4’s.

Singular fits

In this example, the fitted random-effect covariance has reduced rank. Use fit_status() and is_singular() to inspect the result:

fit_status(fit)
#> [1] "converged_reduced_rank"
is_singular(fit)
#> [1] TRUE

diagnostics() gives more detail, and changes() compares the requested model with its effective specification and fitted covariance. See vignette("convergence", package = "mixeff") for the meaning of each status and the consequences for inference.

Available inference methods

inference_options() lists the methods available for a fitted model, explains any restrictions, and gives the function call for each method. The status and reason codes are defined in the inference-method glossary.

opt <- inference_options(fit, "days", nsim = 200)
opt$table[, c("method", "expected_status",
              "expected_reliability_reason", "current")]
#>              method expected_status
#> 1 asymptotic_wald_z       available
#> 2     satterthwaite    not_assessed
#> 3     kenward_roger    not_assessed
#> 4         bootstrap       available
#> 5     bootstrap_lrt    not_assessed
#> 6 cluster_bootstrap    not_assessed
#> 7        profile_ci    not_assessed
#>                      expected_reliability_reason current
#> 1                     asymptotic_wald_z_fallback    TRUE
#> 2          satterthwaite_unavailable_at_boundary   FALSE
#> 3          kenward_roger_unavailable_at_boundary   FALSE
#> 4               bootstrap_monte_carlo_replicates   FALSE
#> 5                      bootstrap_lrt_requires_ml   FALSE
#> 6 bootstrap_cluster_resample_p_value_unavailable   FALSE
#> 7             profile_ci_unavailable_at_boundary   FALSE

For this singular fit, mixeff withholds Satterthwaite and Kenward–Roger tests. Parametric bootstrap tests remain available. The inference vignette explains these restrictions and demonstrates the alternatives: vignette("inference", package = "mixeff").

An inference result includes its method and status. If a requested quantity is unavailable, the function returns a reason code with the result or raises a typed error.

Supported models

supported_models() reads the package’s support registry (inst/support/model-support.json). Tests check that the registry, fitting code, and documentation agree.

sm <- supported_models()
knitr::kable(sm$glmm_families[, c("family", "links", "estimators")],
             caption = "GLMM family/link/estimator cells, from the registry.")
GLMM family/link/estimator cells, from the registry.
family links estimators
binomial logit, probit, cloglog pirls_profiled, joint_laplace
poisson log, sqrt pirls_profiled, joint_laplace
Gamma inverse, log pirls_profiled, joint_laplace
inverse.gaussian inverse, log pirls_profiled, joint_laplace
gaussian log, inverse, sqrt pirls_profiled, joint_laplace
negative_binomial log pirls_profiled 
knitr::kable(sm$features[, c("feature", "lmm", "glmm")],
             caption = "Feature support, from the registry.")
Feature support, from the registry.
feature lmm glmm
case weights supported supported
offset supported supported
simulate supported supported
refit supported supported
subset / na.action / contrasts supported supported
random = (GLMM) not applicable refused
stateful fixed-effect terms (factor(), poly(), scale(), ns()/bs(), cut(), relevel(), offset(), ^, %in%, parenthesised groups) supported supported
marginal means verbs (mm_means / mm_comparisons / mm_grid / mm_predictions / test_effect) supported refused
double-bar || with factor terms supported supported

mixeff does not fit nonlinear mixed models. Only the GLM families and links listed above are supported. The nAGQ > 1 option lets you check how quadrature order affects a profiled-PIRLS fit. It requires a single scalar random effect and is unavailable with the joint-Laplace estimator.

For the full tables, including notes on individual features, see vignette("lme4-migration", package = "mixeff"). When comparing results with lme4, keep two qualifications in mind:

  • Estimates are not bit-for-bit identical to lme4; the criterion is agreement within documented tolerances on the parity datasets shipped with the package. Where results are expected to differ, the differences are classified in inst/extdata/expected-mismatches.json, with tolerances enforced by the test suite.
  • Generalized fits have estimator-specific inference methods; see vignette("glmm", package = "mixeff") for the estimators and vignette("inference", package = "mixeff") for the inference routes.

Saving and restoring a fit

Save a fit with saveRDS() and reload it with readRDS(). The stored coefficients and diagnostics remain available after reloading:

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(fit, path)
restored_fit <- revive(readRDS(path))

identical(fixef(restored_fit),             fixef(fit))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(changes(restored_fit)$table,     changes(fit)$table)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(diagnostics(restored_fit)$table, diagnostics(fit)$table)
#> [1] TRUE

Operations on a restored fit

Stored coefficients, fitted values, variance components, and audit records are available after readRDS() without a live Rust handle. The checks above compare these stored values before and after saving.

New LMM contrasts and term tests, conditional random-effect variances, engine-backed prediction, and prediction uncertainty reuse a live native handle. After serialization, native queries restore the recorded fitted state without running an optimizer. revive() resets the R cache and clears a dead handle; restoration rebuilds matrix factors at the saved parameters. Derivative calculations required by an inference method may still take time.

Restoration requires a matching engine source and build configuration. A fit without a live handle and without a compatible snapshot keeps its stored extractors but refuses native queries that require restoration. Keep the package and engine build with the saved fit when reproducing an analysis. Explicit refitting, bootstrap, profile intervals and convergence verification still perform the optimization those operations request.

fit2 <- lmm(
  score ~ week + treatment + (1 | clinic),
  clinic_visits,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)

path2 <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(fit2, path2)

restored <- readRDS(path2)
restored <- revive(restored)

revive() resets the object’s process-local cache. You can call it after readRDS(), but the extractors and inference functions shown below also work on the plain readRDS() result. Stored extractors read durable values; operations requiring a native model restore the saved state as described above when no live handle remains.

fixef(restored)
#>      (Intercept)             week treatmentcoached 
#>        7.6828778       -0.2783994       -0.8994747
head(predict(restored))
#>        1        2        3        4        5        6 
#> 7.585932 7.307533 7.029134 6.750734 6.472335 6.193935
reporting_table(restored, "fixed_effects")
#>              term   estimate  std_error        df  statistic statistic_name
#>       (Intercept)  7.6828778 0.19646018 12.565500  39.106539              t
#>              week -0.2783994 0.02595083 59.000150 -10.727955              t
#>  treatmentcoached -0.8994747 0.26225014  9.999671  -3.429835              t
#>       p_value        method    status reliability
#>  1.665335e-14 satterthwaite available    moderate
#>  1.776357e-15 satterthwaite available    moderate
#>  6.440574e-03 satterthwaite available    moderate

Conditional variances for random effects can also be requested after reload. The engine restores the saved fit without optimization. With condVar = TRUE, each grouping table in this example carries a finite postVar array.

re <- ranef(restored, condVar = TRUE)
attr(re, "mm_unavailable_reason")
#> NULL
dim(attr(re$clinic, "postVar"))
#> [1]  1  1 12

For details of vcov(), see vignette("inference", package = "mixeff"). Rebuilding design matrices with model.matrix() and getME() is demonstrated in vignette("lmm", package = "mixeff").

Stored records and schemas

The structured JSON artifacts stored in the fitted object are the source of truth; external pointers such as the Rust handle are caches. mm_json_known_schemas() lists the artifact schemas this version of the package understands:

head(mm_json_known_schemas())
#>                                       name version
#> 1                                  formula      v0
#> 2      mixedmodels.compiled_model_artifact       1
#> 3           mixedmodels.model_audit_report       2
#> 4             mixedmodels.random_term_card       1
#> 5 mixedmodels.fixed_effect_inference_table   1.2.0
#> 6      mixedmodels.marginal_quantity_table   1.0.0

Lower-level tools

Most users start with lmm(), glmm(), summary(), contrast(), test_effect(), compare(), and reporting_table(). The lower-level functions are there when you need them:

  • mm_parse_formula() checks formula syntax and returns the canonical spelling (demonstrated in vignette("lmm", package = "mixeff")).
  • compile_model() builds a pre-fit model specification; explain_model() translates it into named forms and plain-language scopes (also in vignette("lmm", package = "mixeff")).
  • diagnostics() and changes() expose model-state checks.
  • mm_json_known_schemas() lists the structured artifact schemas understood by this version of the package.
